items.title: The future of peer review requires AI support, not AI bans
items.author: Xuegong Zhang
items.blurb: With submissions rising and manuscripts growing more complex, a Tsinghua University researcher argues journals should give reviewers sanctioned AI tools rather than blanket bans that are hard to monitor and protect confidentiality only imperfectly.

items.title: More than 18,000 questionable images found in antibody catalogues of 15 companies
items.author: Dan Garisto
items.blurb: A science sleuth's audit of commercial antibody catalogues turned up more than 18,000 suspect images, raising questions for researchers working to improve the reliability of the reagents underpinning much of biomedicine.

items.title: The Western water crisis has a simple solution
items.author: Matthew Yglesias
items.blurb: Yglesias frames the American West's water shortage as a pricing failure: the majority of the water is given away to farmers for almost nothing.

items.title: The everything theory of mass transit
items.blurb: Loading transit agencies with emissions, beautification, union-job and community-input mandates trades off against moving people: the Boston Green Line extension added a $20 million bike path after 13 people asked for one at a community meeting.

items.title: Overreaching causal language in the social sciences
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Large language models were used to scan 194,631 cross-sectional articles for causal claims the study designs cannot support.

items.title: YIMBYs already have a bold vision for solving the housing crisis
items.author: Matthew Yglesias
items.blurb: Yglesias answers critics who call the pro-housing program narrow, arguing there is nothing small about what it proposes.

items.title: Canada poaches 48 US-based top academics
items.blurb: Ottawa's recruitment drive has landed 48 US-based researchers, with the FT crediting the Trump administration's pressure on American universities for the opening.

items.title: The Unwelcoming States of America
items.blurb: The Economist's leader argues that by trying to change America's demographic trajectory, Donald Trump will leave the country weaker.

items.title: British politicians want a manufacturing jobs boom
items.blurb: British politicians across parties want factory employment back; the Economist calls it a poor way to achieve economic growth.

items.title: The economic costs of Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown
items.blurb: The bill for the immigration crackdown, in the Economist's accounting, is a smaller workforce and slower growth.

items.title: Americans Are Spending Luxury Dollars for Dive-Bar Service
items.author: Annie Lowrey
items.blurb: Lowrey argues that onerous government rules levy a tax paid in time, so Americans pay luxury prices for service that leaves them waiting.

items.title: A Society of Cheats
items.author: John Paul Rollert
items.blurb: Rollert argues that students' use of AI is teaching them to cut corners, disdain rules and believe that integrity is for suckers.

items.title: Will anybody use AI as much as coders?
items.blurb: Coders have taken to AI more intensively than anyone else; whether other professions ever catch up has big implications for the investment boom, the Economist argues.

items.title: Scholar Data
items.author: Alex Tabarrok
items.blurb: Tabarrok applies a public-goods test to the NSF's economics funding: the agency's prominent grants look strikingly similar to the research that universities, philanthropy and the market already support.

items.title: Checks and Balance newsletter: Silicon Valley’s simulation idea is old and dull
Rising bond yields add tens of billions to G7 countries’ debt costs
Big Tech profits get $160bn boost from gains on stakes in other AI companies
China fact of the day
items.author: Tyler Cowen

items.title: AI and Employment: So Far, So Good
items.author: Alex Tabarrok
items.blurb: Census Bureau surveys of hundreds of thousands of firms show AI adoption rising fast while 95.7% report no change in total employment — and the changers split almost evenly between increases and decreases, Tabarrok notes.

items.title: The dawn of physical AI
items.blurb: Wall Street and Silicon Valley have high hopes for AI that interacts with the real world, while unions and economists warn of its effects on jobs and wages, the FT reports.

items.title: Democrats should vow to surrender in the Canada trade war
items.author: Matthew Yglesias
items.blurb: Yglesias argues Democrats should pledge to repudiate the Canada trade war entirely, calling that good politics, good policy and a requirement for a peaceful world.

items.title: What’s your lab’s archetype? The answer could inform how you use AI
items.author: Jenna Ahart
items.blurb: A white paper sorts research groups into four archetypes, each of which puts artificial intelligence to work in the lab differently, Nature reports.

items.title: Trump says data centre critics ‘want to end up backwards and poor’
Consultants head for an AI showdown — with their own clients
We Are Living in the Fantasy World of 13-Year-Old Boys
items.author: Gal Beckerman

items.author: Michael Schuman

items.title: Why are rich people so pessimistic? What the numbers say

items.title: ‘Stunning’ Percolation Proof Solves Decades-Old Puzzle About Phase Transitions
items.author: Leila Sloman

items.title: Just bury your trash
items.author: Alex Chalmers and Rob Wiblin
items.blurb: Chalmers and Wiblin make the case that burying most waste in modern landfills beats recycling it — reusable substitutes like the cotton tote can take 173 times the energy of the disposable they replace.

items.title: AI hits college graduates in the heart of America’s data centre boom
items.blurb: Job postings in Texas have dropped for AI-exposed occupations, new research shows, squeezing college graduates in the middle of America’s data-centre building boom.

items.title: More optimistic results on AI and job markets
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Cowen points to a new Hartley, Jolevski, Melo and Moore paper: generative-AI adoption is widespread but substantial aggregate labour-market disruption is not yet visible — even as workers perceive real displacement risk.

items.title: Bland new world: is AI making us all think the same?
items.author: Matthew Hutson
items.blurb: Researchers worry that generative AI is homogenizing culture and cognition, Hutson reports — one computer scientist says he keeps getting déjà vu reading recent papers in his field.

items.title: China’s real robot revolution is not about humanoids
items.blurb: China is applying its superpower of scaling and supply-chain building to industrial robotics, the FT argues — the challenge to the global industry lies there, not in humanoids.

items.title: India has an ambitious plan to lure scientists back — will it work?
items.author: Mohana Basu
items.blurb: New fellowships aim to entice Indian researchers abroad to come home, but scientists tell Nature the schemes offer no long-term income security.
